Title: 2508.10595v1 - On Spectral Properties of Gradient-based Explanation Methods

On Spectral Properties of Gradient-based
Explanation Methods
Amir Mehrpanah1 , Erik Englesson1 , and Hossein Azizpour1
Department of Computer Science, Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
{amirme,engless,azizpour}@kth.se
Abstract. Understanding the behavior of deep networks is crucial to in-
crease our confidence in their results. Despite an extensive body of work
for explaining their predictions, researchers have faced reliability issues,
which can be attributed to insufficient formalism. In our research, we
adopt novel probabilistic and spectral perspectives to formally analyze
explanation methods. Our study reveals a pervasive spectral bias stem-
ming from the use of gradient, and sheds light on some common design
choices that have been discovered experimentally, in particular, the use
of squared gradient and input perturbation. We further characterize how
the choice of perturbation hyperparameters in explanation methods, such
as SmoothGrad, can lead to inconsistent explanations and introduce two
remedies based on our proposed formalism: (i) a mechanism to determine
a standard perturbation scale, and (ii) an aggregation method which we
call SpectralLens. Finally, we substantiate our theoretical results through
quantitative evaluations.
Keywords: Probabilistic Machine Learning · Gradient-based Explana-
tion Methods · Probabilistic Pixel Attribution Techniques · Explainabil-
ity · Deep Neural Networks · Spectral Analysis
1
Introduction
Ensuring the interpretability of machine learning models is crucial for user’s trust
and understanding [2, 6, 45]. While considerable efforts have been dedicated to
advancing explainability in the field [37,47,49,51,57,62], there is a notable gap
in systematically formalizing and consolidating existing knowledge [5,9,16,19].
Insufficient formal analysis leaves too much room for different interpretations of
the explanations, making them unreliable [27] which is detrimental to the very
use case of explanations, i.e., human-critical applications. Therefore, more at-
tention is essential to retrospectively analyze and structure the wealth of work
done, creating a cohesive foundation for explainability [39,61].
One main reason for the unreliability of explanation methods is their suscepti-
bility to hyperparameters, leading to inconsistent explanations [4,13,33,36,48],
see Fig. 1. Among the several works that formally study explanation meth-
ods [19,37,57], to our knowledge, none shed light on such inconsistencies. There-
fore, in this work, we adopt a novel probabilistic and spectral perspective to
characterize the observed inconsistencies and propose preliminary solutions.

Fig. 1: The figure illustrates sample explanations generated by varying hyperparam-
eters of SmoothGrad-Squared [30, 55] for ResNet-50 on ImageNet (see Fig. 16 in the
Appendix for more examples). It is evident from the figure that using different hyper-
parameters results in diverse explanations. Such variations have been demonstrated in
recent studies for other explanation techniques as well [4,13,33,48].
Our Contribution. We iterate our contributions in three parts:
– Analysis: We introduce a probabilistic representation for post-hoc gradient-
based explanation methods in Sec. 2.1, and perform a spectral analysis of
them in Sec. 3.1.
– Identified Issues: Our examination reveals a shared spectral bias stem-
ming from the fundamental assumption of utilizing gradients to measure
feature contributions. We show that the combined spectral effects of gradi-
ent and perturbation lead to band-pass filters modulating the explanations,
which could lead to inconsistencies in the explanations, discussed in Sec. 3.2.
Moreover, we conduct a spectral analysis of a few specific perturbation dis-
tributions that have been proposed in the literature in Sec. 3.3.
– Solutions and Evaluations: To address inconsistencies, we investigate
two straightforward solutions that are finding an optimal perturbation scale
based on the cosine similarity of the perturbation and the classifier in the
frequency domain in Sec. 4.1, and an aggregation mechanism named Spec-
tralLens in Sec. 4.2. Finally, we evaluate the proposed methods using the
pixel removal strategy [48], acknowledging their effectiveness and limitations
under Sec. 5.
2
Background
Notation. We consider a classification setting, that is, modeling p(y|x) for
labels y ∈{1, . . . , k} and x ∈Rn the set of input images. We denote the
log p(y|x) by f. We denote standard Fourier bases by {ψ(ω, x)}ω∈Rn, accord-
ing to which, under some regularity conditions [43], f can be decomposed as
f(x) =
R bf(ω)ψ(ω, x)dω. In this representation, bf denotes the Fourier transform
(FT) of f. We denote the power spectral density (PSD) of f by Sf(ω) = | bf(ω)|2.

Spectral Properties of Gradient-based Explanation Methods
3
2.1
A Probabilistic Representation of Explanations
In this view, each explanation method consists of three components: (1) a dis-
tribution for perturbation of the input, (2) an explainer, and (3) a summary
statistic. We use p(˜x|x, σ) to denote the distribution of perturbations of the
input sample parameterized by σ, referred to as the perturbation scale. A defi-
nition of “explanation” is recovering the contribution of features to a prediction,
which emanates from human’s natural counterfactual reasoning [19]. Therefore,
the explainer is usually the gradient with respect to input ∇x, or approximations
of it, e.g. the finite difference, given by ∆xf(x) = f(˜x)−f(x)
˜x−x
(see Appendix D).
Finally, we assume that the summary statistic is the expectation of the out-
puts, or the squared outputs, of the explainer, e.g. (∇f(˜x))2, over the chosen
perturbation distribution, p(˜x|x, σ), denoted as Ep(˜x)

erations are carried out pixelwise. This is referred to as the explanation of f at
x with a hyperparameter σ. This probabilistic view can, in fact, unify different
explanation methods into a single form (see Appendix C). We provide theo-
retical justifications for why using squared gradients is preferable to gradients,
explaining the empirical findings [30], and will discuss both cases in Sec. 3.1.
3
Spectral Analysis of Explanations
This section demonstrates the spectral property in explanations when using the
gradient explainer and its interaction with perturbations, where a significant
difference in the frequency of learned features leads to a selective attribution of
features. In the following sections, we draw on insights from spectral analysis
of signals and systems theory, utilizing this viewpoint to gain a deeper under-
standing of explanation methods. We demonstrate a spectral bias related to
gradient-based explanation approaches, identify its source, and interpret various
methods in the literature as efforts to alleviate it through the incorporation of
low-pass filters, either explicitly [55,57] or implicitly [42,62]. We illustrate that
the inconsistencies in explanation techniques stem from different strategies for
mitigating the spectral bias. Finally, we suggest two straightforward approaches
to tackle these inconsistencies: determining an optimal perturbation scale in
Sec. 4.1 and aggregating the explanations in Sec. 4.2.
Writing a spectral representation for prediction, as shown in Appendix A.1,
the model output with a perturbation distribution can be written as a convolu-
tion between the function and the perturbation distribution f ∗p, therefore we
may use “perturbation kernel” and “perturbation distribution” interchangeably.

3.2
Gradient Explainers with Perturbations Are Band-Pass Filters
In our probabilistic framework, various explanation methods can be decomposed
into three components (1) an explainer, (2) a perturbation kernel and (3) a
summary statistic. In this section, we analyze the spectral effects of the two
core components, namely gradient and perturbation. Importantly, we show that
gradient acts as a high-pass filter, and perturbation acts as a low-pass filter.
Before that, we need a more formal definition for a high-pass and low-pass filter
that suits our study. Assuming that bm(ω) denotes the FT of a perturbation
kernel, we define low- and high-pass as follows.
Definition 1. A filter bm(ω) is low pass, if for a given M > 0 there exists a
threshold ω∗such that for any ∥ω∥> ∥ω∗∥, we have ∥bm(ω)∥< M, and it is
high pass if such a condition holds for ∥ω∥< ∥ω∗∥.
For better readability, the proofs for the theorems and propositions are out-
lined in Appendix B, and we provide intuition as we progress.
Theorem 1. Any perturbation kernel p(˜x) mitigates the attribution of high-
frequency features; simply put, any perturbation is a low-pass filter.
The intuition is that any modification to a signal, would only remove infor-
mation, and, as the intensity of perturbation increases, the removal goes from
high-frequency components toward lower frequencies.

The paper discusses spectral properties of different explanation methods in machine learning, focusing on gradients and perturbation kernels. For methods utilizing gradients and perturbation kernels, the equation for expected gradient contributions is provided. The Fourier transform of the perturbation kernel, denoted \( \hat{g}_a(\boldsymbol{\omega}) \), impacts how the classifier is decomposed into even and odd parts, influencing the interpretation of attributions. Squared gradients reveal a different spectral property, being always non-negative and reflecting the power spectral density (PSD) of the classifier. These explanations act as band-pass filters; gradients are high-pass, while perturbation kernels are low-pass. This distinction is useful for understanding how different methods highlight or suppress certain frequency components in feature attributions.
